question: Integers \(a\) and \(b\) are randomly chosen without replacement from the set of integers with absolute value not exceeding \(10.\) What is the probability that the polynomial \(x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 6\) has \(3\) distinct integer roots?
solution:
The constant term restricts the integer roots much more sharply than the coefficient bounds do, so begin by listing possible root sets.

If the distinct integer roots are \(p,q,r\), expanding
\[
(x-p)(x-q)(x-r)=x^3+ax^2+bx+6
\]
gives
\[
pqr=-6,\qquad a=-(p+q+r),\qquad b=pq+pr+qr.
\]
The absolute values of the roots are positive integers with product \(6\). Listed in increasing order, the smallest must be \(1\), since three numbers at least \(2\) would have product at least \(8\). The remaining two form a factor pair of \(6\). Thus the only absolute-value patterns are \((1,1,6)\) and \((1,2,3)\).

For \((1,1,6)\), distinctness forces the two roots of absolute value \(1\) to be \(1\) and \(-1\). Their product is \(-1\), so the third root must be \(6\). For \((1,2,3)\), a negative product requires either exactly one negative root or all three negative. These possibilities give the complete table:

| Unordered root set | \(a=-(p+q+r)\) | \(b=pq+pr+qr\) | Allowed? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| \(\{-1,1,6\}\) | \(-6\) | \(-1\) | Yes |
| \(\{1,2,-3\}\) | \(0\) | \(-7\) | Yes |
| \(\{1,-2,3\}\) | \(-2\) | \(-5\) | Yes |
| \(\{-1,2,3\}\) | \(-4\) | \(1\) | Yes |
| \(\{-1,-2,-3\}\) | \(6\) | \(11\) | No |

For example, the second row has \(a=-(1+2-3)=0\) and \(b=2-3-6=-7\). The final row is excluded because \(b>10\). In each of the other four rows, both coefficients lie in \([-10,10]\) and \(a\ne b\), as required by sampling without replacement.

There are \(21\) choices for \(a\), followed by \(20\) choices for \(b\), giving \(420\) equally likely ordered pairs. Root permutations do not produce additional polynomials, and the four valid rows give four different coefficient pairs. Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac4{21\cdot20}=\boxed{\frac1{105}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
